sources.title: Alicia Garza: birth date and movement biography
sources.findings: Read National Women’s History Museum biography: explicit 4 January 1981 birth date, co-founding history and organising work. The birthplace Oakland conflicts with The HistoryMakers indexed biography’s Los Angeles and EBSCO overview’s Marin County; birthplace is omitted, not silently resolved. Avoid adopting charged descriptions of the Martin and Brown cases as findings of criminal guilt.

sources.title: 12 April 2018: alumni profile confirming 2002 graduation and subjects
sources.findings: Read UC San Diego April 2018 alumni profile, specifically Garza’s section: graduation in 2002 in anthropology and sociology. Daniel Caspi’s adjacent Caltech PhD and medical patent are unrelated. The National Domestic Workers Alliance role is historical as of 2018. A claimed 2017 master’s degree lacked a directly verified university record in this review and is not asserted.

sources.title: 17 February 2020: Alicia Garza interview on organising and Black Futures Lab
sources.findings: Read Garza’s interview published by AAIHS on 17 February 2020. Her own account distinguishes leaving BLM Global Network daily operations in 2017 from launching Black Futures Lab in 2018. Community surveys, organiser training and policy participation are described as its work. Tentative book title in the introduction is not the final title; numeric programme claims and future ambitions are not carried forward as current outcomes.

sources.title: Who we are: mission, survey work and distinction from BLM
sources.findings: Read Black Futures Lab’s Who We Are page. It identifies Garza as founder and distinguishes the Lab, BLM Global Network and Movement for Black Lives coalition. Its Black Census Project is an organisational survey, not a federal enumeration. The current homepage also calls her founder and describes a 2026 response target; the target is not a completed count or evidence that she still directs daily operations.

sources.title: 6 February 2024: senior staff appointments
sources.findings: Read original JPB Foundation appointment release dated 6 February 2024. It names Garza among six senior staff additions with the title Senior Vice President of Movement Infrastructure and Explorations. The date is an announcement, not a proven first working day. Bhargava’s presidency, board appointments and foundation-wide grant commitments do not belong to Garza personally.

sources.title: Foundation history and 2024 change of name
sources.findings: Read Freedom Together foundation history: JPB was renamed in 2024, so these are successive names of the same foundation, not two separate employers. Its presidential succession is not Garza’s job history. No foundation grant totals are treated as her personal assets or donations.

sources.title: The Purpose of Power: edition publication dates
sources.findings: Read publisher edition metadata and description: ebook and audiobook dated 20 October 2020; paperback 7 September 2021. Do not substitute the paperback date for original publication or carry the older tentative title forward. Promotional endorsements and bestseller labels are not used as independent evaluations.

sources.title: Our Story: 2019 founding and related education fund
sources.findings: Read Supermajority’s Our Story: 2019 launch with Cecile Richards, Ai-jen Poo and Garza; the related education fund has additional founding collaborators. Use nonexclusive co-founder language and do not confuse these organisational structures. Undated membership totals and stale active-status copy are superseded by its 2026 announcement.

sources.title: 8 January 2026: announcement ending standalone organisation
sources.findings: Read Supermajority’s primary announcement dated 8 January 2026. It states that the organisation will no longer remain standalone and directs members toward local organising and groups including the ACLU. This is not proof of a legal merger, acquisition or insolvency. Do not treat the claim of 20 million voters activated as an independently audited effect or attribute organisational closure to personal misconduct.

sources.title: 2017 Black Lives Matter: award recipient and 2 November ceremony
sources.findings: Read Sydney Peace Foundation’s 2017 recipient and ceremony account. The laureate was the Black Lives Matter Global Network. On 2 November, Patrisse Cullors, Rodney Diverlus and Dawn Modkins accepted on its behalf. Do not claim Garza personally attended or alone received the prize, notwithstanding compressed secondary biographies.

sources.title: 2 June 2026: account of the 19 May symposium and Garza’s keynote
sources.findings: Read MIT Picower Institute’s retrospective published 2 June 2026 describing the actual 19 May symposium. It identifies Garza as Freedom Together senior vice president and describes her keynote, The Politics of Hope. The event and publication dates differ; 300 registrations are not a verified attendance total. Her views on hope are attributed speech, not a neuroscience finding of her own.

sources.title: 23 July 2026: Freedom Table conversation with Alicia Garza and LaTosha Brown
sources.findings: Read Rashad Robinson’s NewsOne article published 23 July 2026. It describes a completed Freedom Table conversation in which Garza guest-hosted Robinson and LaTosha Brown. Exact recording date was not stated; July 23 is publication, not an asserted date of physical appearance. From Presence to Power is Robinson’s book, not Garza’s. No video or audio inspection is claimed.

sources.title: 4 March 2024 lecture account: career and foundation transition
sources.findings: Read Yale Law School’s account of Garza’s 4 March 2024 lecture: National Domestic Workers Alliance special-projects role from 2013 and transition to the JPB Foundation. This corroborates that the February announcement did not mean all prior roles ended that day. The page’s differing Global Justice/Women’s Rights headings are not treated as two events. No law degree or Yale appointment is inferred.
